# Adjudication Task — Chapter 208

## Korean source

```text
  1|＃208화
  2|
  3|
  4|
  5|종횡무진(縱橫無盡).
  6|
  7|지금의 내 모습이 그랬다. 눈에 보이고 손이 닿는 곳마다 거침없이 베고, 찌르고, 박살 냈다. 창날이 번뜩일 때마다 피가 솟구치고 살과 뼈가 갈라졌다.
  8|
  9|나는 아무런 제약도 받지 않고 거대한 오우거들의 사이를 거침없이 누볐다.
 10|
 11|서걱! 콰드드득!
 12|
 13|- 구워어어억!
 14|
 15|단말마와 함께 3m에 달하는 거체가 무릎을 꿇는다.
 16|
 17|게이트는 계속해서 오우거들을 쏟아 냈지만 내게는 아무런 문제도 되지 않았다. 두 마리가 나오면 셋을 죽였고, 세 마리가 나오면 넷을 죽였다.
 18|
 19|‘쉽다. 신기할 정도로.’
 20|
 21|포인트를 적용시켰던 것은 철우와의 비무가 마지막.
 22|
 23|그러나 임독양맥의 타통은 공력의 제어와 폭발력, 그리고 감각을 극도로 상승시켰다.
 24|
 25|엄청난 거력이 담긴 오우거들의 쇠몽둥이가 사방에서 내리꽂혀도 한없이 느리게 보일 뿐이다.
 26|
 27|내 눈에 비친 놈들은 가진 힘을 제대로 활용할 줄 모르는 멍청이에 불과했다.
 28|
 29|쐐애애액! 퍽!
 30|
 31|- 그르르륵…….
 32|
 33|피가래 끓는 소리와 함께 몇 번째인지 모를 오우거가 무릎을 꿇었다.
 34|
 35|자신의 목젖을 정확히 꿰뚫은 창날을 움켜잡으려던 털북숭이 손바닥이 힘을 잃고 툭, 떨어진다.
 36|
 37|띠링.
 38|
 39|
 40|
 41|- [Lv.85 오우거]를 해치웠습니다!
 42|
 43|- 상당량의 경험치를 획득합니다!
 44|
 45|- 레벨 업!
 46|
 47|
 48|
 49|“오.”
 50|
 51|벌써 레벨 업이라니.
 52|
 53|이거 혼자서 쓸어 버리니까 경험치 빨아들이는 속도가 장난이 아니다.
 54|
 55|‘잡는 놈들마다 하나같이 나보다 고레벨이라 그런가.’
 56|
 57|지금 내 레벨이 70대 중후반이니 오우거들과는 적게는 5레벨, 많게는 10레벨 차이다.
 58|
 59|그런 놈들을 정육점 목살처럼 서걱서걱 썰어 버리니 금방 레벨이 오를 수밖에.
 60|
 61|경험치가 생각 이상으로 되게 쏠쏠한데?
 62|
 63|‘아니, 잠깐만.’
 64|
 65|순간 뇌리를 스치는 한 줄기 생각.
 66|
 67|나는 반짝이는 눈으로 꿀렁거리며 오우거를 뱉어 내는 게이트를 바라봤다.
 68|
 69|이거 완전히…….
 70|
 71|‘맛집이잖아.’
 72|
 73|게이트에서는 계속해서 경험치, 아니 몬스터를 뱉어 내고 나는 죽이고. 그렇게 꾸준히 반복한다면?
 74|
 75|‘회전 초밥집이 여기 있었구나.’
 76|
 77|오우거에게서 얻는 경험치는 참치 대뱃살보다 달콤하다.
 78|
 79|나오는 족족 꼭꼭 씹어서 포인트로 소화할 생각에 입꼬리가 올라가던 그때였다.
 80|
 81|우우웅. 투타타타타!
 82|
 83|- 정지, 정지!
 84|
 85|- 강하!
 86|
 87|거센 바람 소리와 함께 날아온 전투 헬기 서너 대가 머리 위를 맴돌더니, 이십여 명의 헌터들이 벼락처럼 떨어져 내렸다.
 88|
 89|슈슈슈슉!
 90|
 91|20m가 넘는 높이. 이 정도면 아무리 마법 장비를 갖춘 헌터라고 해도 무릎에 무리가 가기 마련이다.
 92|
 93|그러나 이번에 나타난 이들은 내가 오기 전 있던 사람들 같은 어중이떠중이들이 아니었다.
 94|
 95|“페더 폴(Feather Fall)”
 96|
 97|마법사의 영창과 함께 허공에서 느껴지는 기의 파동.
 98|
 99|빠르고 거칠게 내리꽂히던 신체가 속도를 늦췄다. 쇠몽둥이를 휘두르려던 오우거들이 타이밍을 놓치고 머뭇거릴 때, 두 번째 마법이 발현되었다.
100|
101|“그리스(Grease)!”
102|
103|- 구워어?
104|
105|쿵! 콰당!
106|
107|남아 있던 네 마리의 오우거가 중심을 잃고 휘청거리거나 주저앉았다.
108|
109|“지금!”
110|
111|외침과 동시에 속도 감속 마법이 해제되며 근접 딜러들이 빛살처럼 날아들었다.
112|
113|죽음을 직감한 오우거들이 낮은 울음소리를 흘린 그 순간이었다.
114|
115|캉! 카가강!
116|
117|“……어?”
118|
119|놈들의 가슴에 막 무기를 꽂아 넣으려던 헌터들이 황당하다는 표정으로 나를 바라봤다.
120|
121|‘이 새끼가 지금 무슨 짓을 한 거지?’
122|
123|‘제정신인가.’
124|
125|딱 그 표정이다.
126|
127|단 한 번의 휘두름으로 헌터들의 공격을 걷어 낸 내가 점잖은 목소리로 말했다.
128|
129|“거, 상도의는 지킵시다.”
130|
131|“…….”
132|
133|이 새끼들이 어디서 다 잡은 몹을 스틸하려고.
134|
135|
136|
137|* * *
138|
139|
140|
141|“그런 일이 있었어?”
142|
143|자초지종을 들은 대위의 말에 헌터 팀장이 고개를 끄덕였다.
144|
145|“예, 제가 지원팀 2년째 하면서 그런 놈은 처음 본다니까요.”
146|
147|“재미있는 사람이네.”
148|
149|“재밌기는. 완전 또라이죠.”
150|
151|“글쎄.”
152|
153|대위는 천천히 주위를 둘러봤다.
154|
155|원래 형태를 찾아볼 수 없을 만큼 무너진 톨게이트, 반파된 도로에는 몬스터들의 피가 점점이 뿌려져 있었다.
156|
157|뒤집히고 부서진 자동차들도 보였지만 몇 대 되지 않는다.
158|
159|“사상자가 몇이나 되지?”
160|
161|군인과 헌터. 비록 신분은 다르지만 둘 다 정부에는 군 지원팀 소속으로 등록되어 있다.
162|
163|상관 격인 대위의 질문에 헌터 팀장이 냉큼 대답했다.
164|
165|“일단 사망 넷. 중상 다섯이요. 더 파악해 봐야 알겠지만.”
166|
167|“사망 넷, 중상 다섯이라.”
168|
169|덤덤하게 읊조린 대위가 말을 이었다.
170|
171|“게이트 발생이 오늘만 두 번째네.”
172|
173|“그러게요. 한 시간 전쯤에 양주 쪽에서 F급 게이트 하나 터졌으니까. 이거 진짜 무슨 일 나는 거 아닌지 모르겠어요.”
174|
175|헌터 팀장의 말에 대위가 혀를 찼다.
176|
177|“야, 정 팀장아.”
178|
179|“네.”
180|
181|“읍내에서 터진 F급 게이트. 출근길 도로 한가운데에서 터진 B급 게이트. 뭐가 더 심각해 보이냐?”
182|
183|“그야…….”
184|
185|“근데 사상자는 F급 게이트 쪽이 더 많았어. 사망자 열 명에 중상은 스물이 넘는다.”
186|
187|“예? 그럴 리가요. 뉴스 속보에서는…….”
188|
189|“축소, 은폐. 너도 2년째면 슬슬 감 잡아야지. 여기가 어떤 곳인지.”
190|
191|대위가 깊은 한숨을 내쉬었다.
192|
193|“우리 입장에서는 백 번 절해도 모자라. 혼자서 대참사를 막은 시민 영웅 아니냐.”
194|
195|“그건 그렇죠. 좀 또라이 같긴 한데.”
196|
197|“정 팀장.”
198|
199|“아, 아니 그게 아니고요. 엄청 강한 또라이라는 거죠. 혼자서 오우거를 열 마리도 넘게 잡았으니까 A급 헌터는 되는 것 같은데.”
200|
201|“어쨌든 말조심해라. 듣는 귀도 많은데.”
202|
203|“다 우리 애들인데 듣는 귀는 무슨…… 아.”
204|
205|대위가 턱짓하는 곳을 바라본 팀장이 인상을 팍 찡그렸다.
206|
207|고가의 카메라를 든 빼빼 마른 중년인이 신난 발걸음으로 그들을 향해 다가오고 있었다.
208|
209|“이야, 유 대위님! 정 팀장! 지금까지 어디 숨어 계셨어? 한참 찾았네.”
210|
211|헌터 팀장이 영 고까운 얼굴로 대답했다.
212|
213|“김 기자님 피해서요.”
214|
215|“어우, 정 팀장은 오늘따라 왜 이렇게 까칠해? 나도 지원팀 소속이야.”
216|
217|“이럴 때만 팀원이고 군종 기잡니까? 평소에는 맨날 숙취에 찌들어 계시더니 특종 하나 잡았다고 너무 좋아하시는 거 아니에요?”
218|
219|움찔한 기자를 대신해서 대위가 나섰다.
220|
221|“그쯤 해. 김 기자님도 앞으로 유의하시고요. 엄연히 사고 현장인데 특종 잡았다고 혼자서 신나 하는 모습이 좋게 보이진 않습니다.”
222|
223|“……큼. 뭐, 앞으로 주의하겠습니다.”
224|
225|대답하면서도 기자의 눈빛은 기대감으로 반짝 빛났다.
226|
227|게이트 발생은 말 그대로 천재지변이나 다름없다. 아니, 어떤 면에서는 천재지변 이상이다.
228|
229|태풍이 한반도를 덮친다고 하면 언제, 어떻게 올지. 어느 지역이 피해를 입을지 예측이라도 할 수 있지만 게이트 생성은 종잡을 수 없기 때문이다.
230|
231|‘하루에 게이트가 두 번 터진 것도 전대미문인데, 심지어 B급 게이트라.’
232|
233|맥없이 뚫린 톨게이트 경비팀과 출근길에 대참사를 막은 이름 모를 헌터의 영웅 같은 등장!
234|
235|그림이 좋다.
236|
237|이미 머릿속에서 스케치를 끝낸 기자는 몸이 잔뜩 달았다.
238|
239|“그래서, 우리 영웅님은 어디 계셔? A급 헌터지? 이름은 뭐래요? 이런 건 좀 신선한 뉴 페이스가 먹히는데.”
240|
241|“뉴 페이스요? 나 참.”
242|
243|눈살을 찌푸린 헌터 팀장이 기자의 등 뒤를 가리켰다.
244|
245|“저기 있습니다. 뉴 페이스.”
246|
247|“어디? 안 보이는데?”
248|
249|아무리 사방을 둘러봐도 번쩍거리는 갑옷을 걸친 영웅의 모습은 보이지 않는다.
250|
251|바쁘게 사고 현장을 수습 중인 군 소속 직원들만 보일 뿐.
252|
253|주위를 바쁘게 훑던 기자의 눈이 딱 멈췄다.
254|
255|“저기, 정 팀장님. 혹시 저 사람이야? 오우거 사체 앞에…….”
256|
257|“츄리닝 바지 입은 사람. 예, 맞습니다.”
258|
259|스슥, 서걱, 서걱.
260|
261|김장하는 것처럼 쭈그려 앉아 솜씨 좋게 지방과 살, 가죽을 분리해 내는 청년의 뒷모습에 기자가 중얼거렸다.
262|
263|“……저건 너무 뉴 페이슨데?”
264|
265|“신선하죠. 원하던 그림 아니에요?”
266|
267|“신선해 보이긴 하네. 오우거 고기가.”
268|
269|“아까부터 저러고 있어요. 직원들이 해 준다는데 손도 못 대게 해요. 다 자기 거라고.”
270|
271|더 웃긴 건 도축 솜씨가 기가 막히게 좋다는 것이다. 실제로 도축 담당 직원 둘은 힐끗거리며 그의 손놀림을 따라 하는 중이었다.
272|
273|“A급 헌터 맞아?”
274|
275|“글쎄요. 혼자서 오우거를 쓸어 버릴 정도면 분명한데 보면 볼수록 영.”
276|
277|“정 팀장이 물어봤는데, 우선 도축 끝내고 얘기하자더군요.”
278|
279|세 사람이 믿음과 불신이 뒤섞인 눈빛을 교환하던 그때였다.
280|
281|“휴, 끝났다.”
282|
283|그토록 질기다는 오우거 고기를 고등어처럼 토막 낸 A급 헌터가 허리를 펴고 일어났다.
284|
285|무릎이 늘어난 트레이닝복 바지에 삼선 슬리퍼를 본 기자가 중얼거렸다.
286|
287|“돈도 많이 버는 인간이 왜 저러고 산대.”
288|
289|이게 기만인가?
290|
291|어이가 없었지만 한편으로는 볼수록 신선했다. 뭐니 뭐니 해도 미디어에서 가장 중요한 건 캐릭터니까.
292|
293|‘소탈하고 정의감 투철한 A급 헌터라, 이거 그림은 잘 뽑히겠는데? 얼굴도 시원시원하니 잘생겼고.’
294|
295|그래, 번듯하고 모범생 같은 이미지보다 차라리 이게 더 낫다.
296|
297|기자는 씩 웃으며 카메라를 들었다.
298|
299|설정이 하나도 들어가 있지 않은 자연스러운 컷을 따기 위해서였다.
300|
301|
302|
303|* * *
304|
305|
306|
307|‘역시 오우거야. 버릴 게 없지.’
308|
309|나는 깔끔하게 분리된 부산물을 보며 흡족한 미소를 머금었다.
310|
311|오우거는 말 그대로 힘의 상징 같은 존재라 남성들에게 인기가 많다.
312|
313|찾는 사람은 많은데 엄연히 B급 최상위로 분류되는 몬스터인지라 공급은 부족한 편이었다.
314|
315|‘급소만 찌르길 잘했다.’
316|
317|콧노래를 흥얼거리며 부산물을 분류하던 그때였다.
318|
319|찰칵.
320|
321|“……응?”
322|

# Mastering Adjudicator Brief

You are a **veto**, not a second novelist and not a gloss writer.

This call is isolated, non-interactive, and tool-free. The packet already contains the Korean source, both complete English versions, glossary matches, rules, and every numbered hunk. Do not call tools, search the repository, or read files. Do not announce a plan.

The first editor (SOL) has already rewritten the accepted English (BASELINE) for fluency. Default is `SOL`. Take `BASE` only when SOL is actually unfaithful. Write `REPAIR` only when **both** BASE and SOL are unfaithful.

## Default

Choose `SOL` unless a veto below fires.

Keep SOL when it is slangier, punchier, more spoken, or more idiomatic and the Korean sense holds (`기만질` → “con me”, `톡톡히` → “full Peak Master treatment”, `득실거리다` → “crawling with”, `인간 백정` → “butcher of men”, `한 몸` → “are one”, `시원하다` in a bath → “That’s the stuff”, `어렵게 찾아오고 쉽게 깨지는 법` → “hard-won and easily broken”). **Literal closeness to Korean wording is not fidelity.** Preserve the source’s meaning and effect in natural English.

## Veto — choose `BASE`

Use `BASE` only for a real miss:

* wrong denotation, quantity, hedge, category, subject/object, or physical action
* a different English idiom than the Korean joke (`까발리다` ≠ “gives someone away”; `넉살` ≠ “banter”)

## Critical binding translation rules

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

## Footnotes

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;
- a deliberately literal rendering whose cultural or linguistic force would otherwise be lost.

For example, render `고시원` as “goshiwon” when the setting or connotations matter, with a concise footnote explaining that it is a very small, inexpensive room-for-rent housing arrangement. Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.

## Spoilers and Scope

- Safe profiles contain only facts revealed through the latest completed chapter.

- Future knowledge may prevent contradiction but may not add early names, pronouns, certainty, motives, or foreshadowing.

“…Ahem. I’ll be more careful.”

[P111]

[P112]
It was a great story.

[P141]

[P142]

[P143]

[P144]

[P151]

[P152]

[P153]
Click.

[P154]
“…Huh?”

[P155]

[P156]

[P157]
“Oh dear, did I startle you?”

[P158]
*What the hell is with this guy?*

[P159]

[P160]
“You might be once you’re in tomorrow’s newspaper.”

[P161]
“The newspaper?”

[P162]
“Ah, I haven’t introduced myself yet. Here, let’s start with my business card.”

[P163]

[P164]
“Military correspondent.”

[P165]

[P166]
“Ah, yes.”

[P167]
“And the two gentlemen coming up behind me are from the support team as well.”

[P168]
The reporter smiled and gave me a thumbs-up as two men approached from behind him.

[P169]
One wore a Special Forces uniform and the other wore armor. They were, well, dressed like your stereotypical soldier and Hunter.

[P170]
“Nice to meet you. I’m Captain Yoo Sijin, Team Leader of Support Team 25.”

[P171]
“Ah, yes.”

[P172]
*For some reason, that sounded like a name the sun might regret.*[^2]

[P173]
I tilted my head and exchanged introductions with the two men.

[P174]

[P175]

[P176]
“Yes. Why?”

[P181]
“What?”

[P182]

[P183]
“…”

[P184]

[P185]
*This is fun.*

[P186]
*After getting knocked around in another world, I hide my strength in reality.*

[P187]
That would make a decent novel title.

[P188]

[P189]

[P192]

[P194]

[P195]

[P196]

[P197]
I had just remembered something I’d momentarily forgotten.

[P198]

[P199]
Damn it. I’m late.

# Mastering Adjudicator Brief

You are a **veto**, not a second novelist and not a gloss writer.

This call is isolated, non-interactive, and tool-free. The packet already contains the Korean source, both complete English versions, glossary matches, rules, and every numbered hunk. Do not call tools, search the repository, or read files. Do not announce a plan.

The first editor (SOL) has already rewritten the accepted English (BASELINE) for fluency. Default is `SOL`. Take `BASE` only when SOL is actually unfaithful. Write `REPAIR` only when **both** BASE and SOL are unfaithful.

## Default

Choose `SOL` unless a veto below fires.

Keep SOL when it is slangier, punchier, more spoken, or more idiomatic and the Korean sense holds (`기만질` → “con me”, `톡톡히` → “full Peak Master treatment”, `득실거리다` → “crawling with”, `인간 백정` → “butcher of men”, `한 몸` → “are one”, `시원하다` in a bath → “That’s the stuff”, `어렵게 찾아오고 쉽게 깨지는 법` → “hard-won and easily broken”). If SOL already naturalized Korean syntax (`이 혁무진` → “I, Hyuk Mujin”), keep SOL. Do not reproduce Korean word order.

**Literal closeness to Korean wording is not fidelity.** Preserve the source’s meaning and effect in natural English.

## Veto — choose `BASE`

Use `BASE` only for a real miss:

* wrong denotation, quantity, hedge, category, subject/object, or physical action
* a different English idiom than the Korean joke (`까발리다` ≠ “gives someone away”; `넉살` ≠ “banter”)

## Critical binding translation rules

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

## Footnotes

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;
- a deliberately literal rendering whose cultural or linguistic force would otherwise be lost.

For example, render `고시원` as “goshiwon” when the setting or connotations matter, with a concise footnote explaining that it is a very small, inexpensive room-for-rent housing arrangement. Define a term at its first meaningful occurrence and do not repeat the note unnecessarily. Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.

- Safe profiles contain only facts revealed through the latest completed chapter.

- Future knowledge may prevent contradiction but may not add early names, pronouns, certainty, motives, or foreshadowing.

 18|

 34|

“You’re only part of the team at times like this, huh? The rest of the time, you’re a military correspondent. You’re usually drowning in a hangover, and now you’re beside yourself just because you landed a scoop.”

[P104]
The reporter flinched, and the captain stepped in.

[P105]
“That’s enough. And Reporter Kim, please be more mindful in the future. This is an accident scene. Running around by yourself in high spirits because you found a scoop doesn’t look good.”

[P106]
“…Ahem. I’ll be more careful.”

[P107]
Even as he answered, anticipation gleamed in the reporter’s eyes.

[P108]
A Gate occurrence was nothing short of a natural disaster. In some ways, it was even worse.

[P109]
If a typhoon was going to strike the Korean Peninsula, people could at least predict when and how it would arrive and which areas might be damaged. There was no predicting where or when a Gate would form.

[P110]
*Two Gates in one day was already unprecedented, and one of them was even B-rank.*

[P111]
A tollgate security team helplessly overrun, followed by the heroic arrival of an unknown Hunter who prevented a rush-hour catastrophe!

[P112]
It was a great story.

[P113]
The reporter had already sketched the whole article out in his head, and he was itching to get started.

[P114]
“So where’s our hero? He’s an A-rank Hunter, right? What’s his name? A fresh new face would sell better for a story like this.”

[P115]
“A new face? Give me a break.”

[P116]
The Hunter Team Leader pointed behind the reporter.

[P117]
“He’s over there. Your new face.”

[P118]
“Where? I don’t see him.”

[P119]
No matter how much he looked around, there was no sign of a hero clad in gleaming armor.

[P120]
All he could see were military personnel busily cleaning up the accident scene.

[P121]
The reporter’s eyes swept across the area before suddenly stopping.

[P122]
“There, Team Leader Jeong. Is that him? In front of the ogre corpse…”

[P123]
“The man in the sweatpants? Yes, that’s him.”

[P124]
Swish. Srrk, srrk.

[P125]
Squatting as if he were making a huge batch of kimchi,[^1] the young man deftly separated the fat, meat, and hide from the corpse. The reporter muttered,

[P126]
“…Now *that’s* a new face.”

[P127]
“Fresh, right? Isn’t that the picture you wanted?”

[P128]
“The ogre meat certainly looks fresh.”

[P129]
“He’s been at it for a while. The staff offered to do it for him, but he won’t let them touch anything. Says it’s all his.”

[P130]
Even funnier, his butchering technique was unbelievably good. The two employees assigned to process the corpses kept sneaking glances at his hands and copying his movements.

[P131]
“Is he really an A-rank Hunter?”

[P132]
“Who knows? He must be if he can wipe out ogres by himself, but the longer I look at him, the less convinced I am.”

[P133]
“I asked him, but he said we could talk after he finished butchering.”

[P134]
The three men exchanged looks filled with equal parts belief and doubt.

[P135]
That was when—

[P136]
“Whew. Finished.”

[P137]
The A-rank Hunter, who had chopped up the notoriously tough ogre meat as easily as a mackerel, straightened his back and stood.

[P138]
The reporter took in his sweatpants, baggy at the knees, and his three-striped slides, then muttered,

[P139]
“Why does a guy who makes that much money live like this?”

[P140]
*Was this some kind of humblebrag?*

[P141]
It was absurd, yet the longer the reporter looked, the more novel the whole thing seemed. After all, nothing mattered more in the media than character.

[P142]
*A down-to-earth A-rank Hunter with a fierce sense of justice. This will make a great story. He’s handsome, too, with bold, clean-cut features.*

[P143]
Yes, this was much better than some polished model-student image.

[P144]
The reporter grinned and raised his camera.

[P145]
He wanted a natural shot with no staging whatsoever.

[P146]
* * *

[P147]
*That’s an ogre for you. Not a single part goes to waste.*

[P148]
I looked over the neatly separated by-products with a satisfied smile.

[P149]
Ogres were practically symbols of strength, which made them popular among men.

[P150]
There were plenty of customers, but because ogres were classified among the highest tier of B-rank monsters, the supply was limited.

[P151]
*Good thing I only went for their vital spots.*

[P152]
I was humming as I sorted the by-products when—

[P153]
Click.

[P154]
“…Huh?”

[P155]
I turned toward the mechanical sound that had come out of nowhere.

[P156]
A middle-aged man repeatedly pressing his camera shutter smiled amiably at me.

[P157]
“Oh dear, did I startle you?”

[P158]
*What the hell is with this guy?*

[P159]
I stared at him incredulously. “Most people are surprised when someone takes their picture without permission. You expect me to be happy about it?”

[P160]
“You might be once you’re in tomorrow’s newspaper.”

[P161]
“The newspaper?”

[P162]
“Ah, I haven’t introduced myself yet. Here, let’s start with my business card.”

[P163]
I accepted the military-camouflage business card and read it aloud.

[P164]
“Military correspondent.”

[P165]
“You know the Capital Defense Command, right? I’m the military correspondent assigned to Support Team 25.”

[P166]
“Ah, yes.”

[P167]
“And the two gentlemen coming up behind me are from the support team as well.”

[P168]
The reporter smiled and gave me a thumbs-up as two men approached from behind him.

[P169]
One wore a Special Forces uniform and the other wore armor. They were, well, dressed like your stereotypical soldier and Hunter.

[P170]
“Nice to meet you. I’m Captain Yoo Sijin, Team Leader of Support Team 25.”

[P171]
“Ah, yes.”

[P172]
*For some reason, that sounded like a name the sun might regret.*[^2]

[P173]
I tilted my head and exchanged introductions with the two men.

[P174]
The perfunctory introductions and praise for my heroic deed had barely ended when the military correspondent, who had been staring at me with fervent eyes, spoke up.

[P175]
“You said you’re Hunter Jin Taekyung, correct?”

[P176]
“Yes. Why?”

[P177]
“Given the field I cover, I know nearly every A-rank Hunter. But…”

[P178]
Ah, I had a pretty good idea what he was trying to say.

[P179]
It was something I would have to deal with sooner or later.

[P180]
I answered readily, “I’m not A-rank.”

[P181]
“What?”

[P182]
“And I’m not S-rank either, of course.”

[P183]
“…”

[P184]
Question marks seemed to appear on all three faces at once. I couldn’t help chuckling.

[P185]
*This is fun.*

[P186]
*After getting knocked around in another world, I hide my strength in reality.*

[P187]
That would make a decent novel title.

[P188]
When I merely smiled without answering, the reporter spoke in a faltering voice.

[P189]
“Th-Then perhaps you’re B-rank?”

[P190]
“No. I’m C-rank.”

[P191]
“…C-rank? You mean C-rank, not C-cup?”

[P192]
“Yes.”

[P193]
*What kind of bullshit is C-cup? And why the hell is he looking at my chest?*

[P194]
Ignoring the waves of disbelief washing over me, I continued, “I was on my way to the Guild when a Gate happened to open…”

[P195]
“Th-Then what?”

[P196]
I couldn’t answer the reporter’s urgent question.

[P197]
I had just remembered something I’d momentarily forgotten.

[P198]
“…By any chance, what time is it?”

[P199]
Damn it. I’m late.

[P200]
[^1]: Kimchi-making, especially in large batches, is traditionally a communal household activity in Korea.

[P201]
[^2]: Captain Yoo Si-jin is the name of the male lead in the Korean drama *Descendants of the Sun*.

# Mastering Adjudicator Brief

You are a **veto**, not a second novelist and not a gloss writer.

This call is isolated, non-interactive, and tool-free. The packet already contains the Korean source, both complete English versions, glossary matches, rules, and every numbered hunk. Do not call tools, search the repository, or read files. Do not announce a plan.

The first editor (SOL) has already rewritten the accepted English (BASELINE) for fluency. Default is `SOL`. Take `BASE` only when SOL is actually unfaithful. Write `REPAIR` only when **both** BASE and SOL are unfaithful.

## Default

Choose `SOL` unless a veto below fires.

Keep SOL when it is slangier, punchier, more spoken, or more idiomatic and the Korean sense holds (`기만질` → “con me”, `톡톡히` → “full Peak Master treatment”, `득실거리다` → “crawling with”, `인간 백정` → “butcher of men”, `한 몸` → “are one”, `시원하다` in a bath → “That’s the stuff”, `어렵게 찾아오고 쉽게 깨지는 법` → “hard-won and easily broken”). If SOL already naturalized Korean syntax (`이 혁무진` → “I, Hyuk Mujin”), keep SOL. Do not reproduce Korean word order.

**Literal closeness to Korean wording is not fidelity.** Preserve the source’s meaning and effect in natural English.

## Veto — choose `BASE`

Use `BASE` only for a real miss:

* wrong denotation, quantity, hedge, category, subject/object, or physical action
* a different English idiom than the Korean joke (`까발리다` ≠ “gives someone away”; `넉살` ≠ “banter”)
* a rebuilt joke whose comic machine BASE already has (`얼마나 …는지 …겠다` must stay a simple exaggeration: “snored so loudly even my mother in Ilsan probably heard him,” not “You had to wonder how loudly…”)
* dropped image, attitude, or timing
* SOL replaces an established project rendering, System label, or Markdown convention with an unsupported synonym
* SOL stamps `hyung` (or another kinship title) onto every narrative name when BASE already uses the name and the Korean `형` is ordinary reference, not a vocative or a topical joke (`진호 형` → Jinho in narration)

Do not veto SOL for being informal. Do not veto SOL to “clarify” slang. Do not veto SOL merely because BASELINE is already understandable.

## `REPAIR` only when both fail

Example: `겹경사가 따로 없다` means two good things **together** (double blessing). `따로` is not “separate.” If BASE says “entirely separate stroke of luck” and SOL says “unexpected windfall,” `REPAIR` to stacked luck.

## Critical binding translation rules

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

## Footnotes

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;
- a deliberately literal rendering whose cultural or linguistic force would otherwise be lost.

For example, render `고시원` as “goshiwon” when the setting or connotations matter, with a concise footnote explaining that it is a very small, inexpensive room-for-rent housing arrangement. Prefer the best natural English analogy in the prose. Use a literal translation plus a concise footnote when the Korean wording itself matters. Define a term at its first meaningful occurrence and do not repeat the note unnecessarily. Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.

## Spoilers and Scope

- Safe profiles contain only facts revealed through the latest completed chapter.
- Never read `characters/spoilers/` during drafting. Reviewers may consult one relevant sealed profile only for a specific unresolved continuity issue after the draft is complete.
- Future knowledge may prevent contradiction but may not add early names, pronouns, certainty, motives, or foreshadowing.
- Translate exactly one requested chapter unless the user explicitly requests a batch. Never modify Korean source files under `source/`.
